symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Run global-route congestion heatmap overlay on the placed DB to see if density is genuinely clean or only locally dense
first_checks.why_first: cheapest; rules out the most common cause (placement density lied)

first_checks.check: Inspect the failing GCell region for pin density / high-fanout nets on the same layer
first_checks.why_first: rules out pin-limited congestion masquerading as routing congestion

first_checks.check: Compare cell row utilization vs. effective density, and check for blocked placement due to macros, blockage, or large hard macros
first_checks.why_first: rules out 'clean-looking but actually blocked' placement

first_checks.check: Check the layer utilization between two adjacent metal layers in the failing region
first_checks.why_first: rules out layer-promotion issues when one layer is saturated

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Look at whether the failing GCell region contains a high-fanout clock/reset/scan net
Look at whether removing the failing block from congestion (or detaching it) clears DRCs elsewhere nearby
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global density or tool tuning issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether DRCs spread across all layers or only at a specific layer transition
Check the experiment using the actual congestion analysis versus a placer-estimated density
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: false alarm from placer's density estimate

common_root_causes.cause: Macro or IP placement blocks region and causes re-routing around it
High-fanout net (clock/reset/scan) topology creating hot spots
Layer assignment or track utilization mismatch (e.g., too many pins on lower metal)
Cell row utilization reporting was misleading; global route finds true hot spots
Wrong routing blockage layer setting in the flow

classic_trap: Trusting the placer's reported utilization as a true picture of the placed design without checking the actual routing congestion heatmap.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, the routable area is dominated by pin accessibility and track pattern, so pin density > cell density often dominates congestion.

first_checks.check: Look at skew report and whether clock latency targets are met on the failing paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock skew as the cause in seconds

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing paths cluster around specific clock-gating cells or the CTS tap point
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock-tree-architecture issues

first_checks.check: Check whether CTS was done with a netlist that includes all clock cells and is consistent with the post-CTS netlist
first_checks.why_first: rules out the common 'clock cells missing in CTS view' mistake

first_checks.check: Look at the cell delay transition time (slew) on the launching/capturing clock pins
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock-buffer slew degradation masquerading as setup

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failing paths share one or a few clock-gating cells with high insertion delay, it's skew/latency root cause; if they spread across hierarchies, check transition times or netlist issues
If launch/capture skew is large only on the failing paths, run skew-opt with finer granularity or balance skew across more levels
Look at the path with timing path mode single-clock vs inter-clock
Check whether CTS treated the failing clock as a leaf or propagated its own delay target

common_root_causes.cause: Excessive clock skew from unbalanced clock tree
Clock-gating cells with high latency and skewed taps
Clock tree doesn't include some clock cells (set_clock_groups or clock-view mismatch)
Transition time degradation on long clock lines or large cells driving clock pins
Operating condition or analysis view mismatch (e.g., worst-case vs typical, multi-mode analysis missing)

classic_trap: Treating setup violations as a data-path problem (re-sizing cells) when the actual cause is clock skew from gating/CTS architecture.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, clock tree resistance matters much more and clock-buffer-only fix doesn't suffice; need to balance drive strength and wire length.

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing paths share a common clock-pinning cell or skew group
first_checks.why_first: rules out skewed clock root cause in seconds

first_checks.check: Run skew-opt for hold only (a hold fix) and see if violations are easily resolvable
first_checks.why_first: rules in/out whether it's an 'easy hold' or a deeper issue

first_checks.check: Check the data-path for high-drive buffers and short data delays on the failing paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out 'too-fast data' common cause

first_checks.check: Look at the scan chain / DFT mode in which holds are reported and verify the mode is realistic
first_checks.why_first: rules out a mode-mismatch root cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing paths originate at the same clock-launch point with short data delay, it's skewed clock; if they span random origins, it's data path
Run hold-fixing with only delay-cell insertion and observe whether the violation magnitude matches expected delay
Compare across analysis modes (functional vs scan) to see whether violations appear in both
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: real chip issue vs scan-only artifact

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If many holds share one endpoint, check that the common endpoint is the same clock-capture pin

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew from CTS architecture (skewed launch/capture on a common clock)
Data path is too fast (large buffer, short wire, transition time very tight)
Hold-fixing was not run / not converged in a previous step
Wrong mode being reported (e.g., DFT scan mode with unrealistic skew)
Operating condition not matching silicon (best-case vs worst-case analysis confusion)

classic_trap: Adding hold buffers everywhere without first checking the clock skew—often the skew imbalance is so large that data path fix never closes.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, hold violations often appear even on the same clock due to local variation; need a finer hold-skew budget and local variation-aware analysis.

first_checks.check: Run static IR-drop analysis on the failing block in the failing mode
first_checks.why_first: cheapest; rules out the entire class

first_checks.check: Check the package/PG-pin density and bump map coverage over the failing region
first_checks.why_first: rules out package-bump-driven IR drop

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing paths cluster around a power-starved region (visualize on the layout)
first_checks.why_first: rules out local power-grid weakness

first_checks.check: Check the activity of the failing paths' cells (toggle rate, frequency, switching probability)
first_checks.why_first: rules out whether IR drop is being modeled with realistic activity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failing paths cluster in a bump-weak region and activity there is high, it's power-grid weak; if they spread out, it's global IR drop or activity too high
Run with raised/lower supply and see if the same paths fail, or if they shift location
Run analysis with a power-grid-only model vs full parasitic to see whether delay correlates with the local mesh voltage
Cross-check dynamic vs static IR drop for the same region

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient bump density or missing power straps over a region
Activity factor too high in the analysis (toggle rate, switching prob too aggressive)
Power-grid resistance too high for the design current (especially in advanced nodes)
Dynamic IR drop from simultaneous switching not modeled in static analysis
Wrong VDD/VSS supply assumed in analysis (analysis library mismatch)

classic_trap: Treating IR-drop-induced delay as a data-path slack problem and re-sizing cells, when the actual fix is power-grid strengthening.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, local dynamic IR drop from simultaneous switching is the dominant cause more than at 28nm, and bumps/straps are denser; static-only analysis often misses it.

symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Check whether the CTS trace shows taps within the allowed target latency range
first_checks.why_first: rules out whether the issue is local or systemic

first_checks.check: Check the DRC/shorts/congestion around the clock tree cells
first_checks.why_first: rules out placement-driven skew divergence

first_checks.check: Check whether the missed sinks share a common region (e.g., far from the clock root or blocked by a macro)
first_checks.why_first: rules out a region-specific root cause

first_checks.check: Look at the clock target spec file to verify the targets are feasible given the topology
first_checks.why_first: rules out over-tight target

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all missed sinks are in one cluster near a macro or hard block, it's placement blockage; if they spread across the chip, it's CTS strategy or netlist
Run a quick local CTS with relaxed targets and see if the same sinks can be reached
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: target too tight, the topology is fine
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: unreachable due to blockage or netlist

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check the clock spec for leaf-sink cells (gates, ICG, multi-cycle paths) and see if they map correctly to clock sources
Run incremental CTS on the failing subtree only and observe if the divergence is in one branch or many

common_root_causes.cause: Blockage / macro placement constraining the clock tree, forcing detour and skew
Over-tight skew target relative to topology
Unbalanced clock tree due to irregular placement (e.g., one side with many sinks)
Netlist inconsistencies (e.g., clock view, set_clock_groups, or clock cell missing)
CTS tool license / config (e.g., wrong reference inverter or buffer strength)

classic_trap: Trying to balance skew further when the real issue is macro blockage forcing a long detour on one side; the right fix is partial block re-placement or spare-space reservation.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, the clock tree must use thicker wire, and many more buffers are needed; single-buffer fixes rarely help—need to plan clock topology before placement.

symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Look at the LVS error log for the exact net name and pin position; locate the source on schematic vs layout
first_checks.why_first: cheapest; rules out most trivial causes

first_checks.check: Check whether the issue is at the top cell or in a leaf cell (top cell LVS report often points there)
first_checks.why_first: rules out leaf-cell vs top mismatch

first_checks.check: Check whether the offending net is a power/ground net (PG net handling often misleads LVS)
first_checks.why_first: rules out common PG-net issue

first_checks.check: Check for fill, ECO, or post-route LVS-only additions not back-annotated to schematic
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common cause in incremental flows

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If the missing net appears in extracted LVS but not in schematic, it's an ECO/buffer added late; if the net exists in schematic but not in layout, it's a route disconnect
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: ECO-vs-schematic mismatch vs real layout open

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If the open net is a power/ground net crossing the cell boundary, it may be missing vias or a sub-PG issue
Check the cell-pin / port-mapping table for the failing cells; mismatches indicate property file issue
Run ERC separately (only connectivity) and compare to LVS; ERC-only mismatches suggest PG-net handling

common_root_causes.cause: Late ECO buffer/inverter added in layout but not back-annotated to netlist
Power/ground net special handling (PG net shorted or merged in LVS but separate in schematic)
Missing via or partial route (open net)
Property file / CDL / pin-mapping issue (pin name mismatch between layout and schematic)
